tagline: Prairies, lakes and country roads connect the landscape of Rawlings’s writing.
intro: South of Gainesville, the Old Florida Heritage Highway combines Scenic US 441 with loop and spur roads through woods, pasture, small lakes and prairies. Florida’s scenic-highway program designated the 45-mile byway on June 7, 2001, and places Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings’s Cross Creek home at the center of its cultural heritage. Along CR 325 and CR 346, the roadside countryside shelters wintering sandhill cranes. The program highlights Micanopy, Rochelle, Evinston and Cross Creek as historic communities along the corridor, together with Paynes Prairie and Lake Wauburg.

Florida built US 441 through the Paynes Prairie basin in 1927, the same year Camp Ranch built canals diverting incoming water toward Orange Lake. Cross Creek’s roads remained unpaved when Rawlings arrived in 1928. CR 325 was paved after World War II; River Styx Road to Micanopy, CR 346, followed in 1962. Electricity reached Cross Creek in 1948.

Begin the loop-and-spur journey at Rochelle, a former railway junction with lines to Gainesville, Ocala and Palatka. At Cross Creek, CR 325 crosses the waterway joining Lochloosa and Orange lakes. Rawlings’s home stands on Orange Lake’s eastern shore. The western leg takes in McIntosh on US 441, then Micanopy and Paynes Prairie between Micanopy and Gainesville.

moments.title: Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings Historic State Park
moments.text: A nineteenth-century dogtrot house forms the core of Rawlings’s home, a single-story wood-frame building on Orange Lake’s eastern shore. Rawlings and her husband Charles enlarged and adapted the house for their use. The property they bought included an orange grove and the old dogtrot house. She lived and worked at Cross Creek from 1928 to 1953, writing The Yearling here. The novel won the Pulitzer Prize in 1939. After her death, the property passed to a University of Florida foundation; the house opened to the public in 1970. Her home and farm now form part of the historic state park. Among the outbuildings, the pump house also dates to the nineteenth century; the barn and tenant house are later structures.

moments.title: Micanopy
moments.text: Micanopy’s historical museum occupies the Thrasher Warehouse, built in 1896 and served by a railroad branch until the 1950s. Before the 1880s, local produce, including citrus, traveled to the southern shore of Lake Alachua, then crossed by boat to railway connections on the northern shore. The Florida Southern Railway brought a branch into Micanopy in 1883, connecting it to the Rochelle-to-Ocala line. The warehouse now houses displays of town history, including William Bartram’s travels and the Seminole Wars. The downtown historic district contains 35 historic buildings and entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1983.

moments.title: Paynes Prairie
moments.text: The savanna crossed by US 441 has also been a steamboat route. Between 1871 and 1891, water filled the basin while Alachua Sink, its principal drain, was blocked. Shallow-draft steamers traveled Alachua Lake, and the sudden draining in 1891 left one stranded. Later canals altered the flow of water into and through the prairie. Florida acquired the land in 1970 and began restoring a more natural environment. US 441 crosses the preserve with a scenic outlook ramp. Within the park, a fifty-foot observation tower near the visitor center provides a view across the preserve.
